newsitem.title: USA: U.S. appeals court dismisses line-item veto lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. appeals court dismisses line-item veto lawsuit.

text.p: A federal appeals court Friday dismissed on technical grounds a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the line-item veto law that President Clinton signed in April.

The three-judge panel upheld a ruling by a lower court judge in July that the National Treasury Employees Union lacked legal standing to bring the lawsuit now. The law does not take effect until January.

The law will allow Clinton to strike selectively spending items to which he objects, instead of having to sign or veto an appropriations bill in full. Just like vetoes of entire bills, a line-item veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress.

The union, which represents workers at Treasury Department agencies, charged the law unconstitutionally shifts power from Congress to the president and "upsets the Constitution's carefully crafted scheme of checks and balances."

Judge David Sentelle wrote in the appeals court ruling that the union had failed to allege any concrete injury from the law, and said there was no "justiciable controversy," meaning the case was not yet ready for a decision.
